name: Wei Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead hand on a crew that puts up mass-timber buildings, big glued wooden panels made in a factory that we crane into place and screw together. Right now it's a new primary school on the edge of town, three storeys of timber. I start at seven with the crane driver going over the lift plan, then it's eight hours of guiding panels in, levelling, fixing and checking. The best bit is when a whole floor goes up in two days and the client walks in and smells the wood. The worst bit is wind, because you can't fly a panel in a gale.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where do computers and AI fit into that day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: More than people think. I use an AI assistant every day to check the panel sequence against the drawings, write up method statements, the documents that say how we'll do a risky job safely, and sort my material lists. I got into it early because I like gadgets and I hate paperwork. My boyfriend Tom is a freelance graphic designer who also teaches an evening class, so between us we talk about AI over dinner more than is healthy. We rent, and we've got about five months of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but in the other direction, because I was the one telling the crew it would change everything. I'd post something honest, like, fair enough, the tools are useful but they weren't magic. Then I'd keep using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my day stays the same, which honestly is a good day. Mass timber is growing anyway because it's greener, so there's plenty of work. It would be good for Tom too, because his clients would stop asking whether a machine can do his logos for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep running my crew and keep using the assistant for paperwork. Finish the crane supervisor course I've already booked for spring, because that's a pay rise either way. And probably start saving for a deposit properly, maybe 400 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit relieved for Tom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said mass timber is growing anyway. How sure are you of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty sure. Every council wants low-carbon schools now and our firm has a two-year order book. I'm the rare builder who'd be a bit disappointed if AI fizzled, and still have more work than I can handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit, because it keeps climbing and we'd like our own place. And my back, which isn't great after ten years of lifting. Nothing that keeps me awake.

say: I'd admit online that the tools were **useful but not magic**.
I'd keep telling the crew the **assistant** still saves paperwork time.
think: My days stay good, since **mass timber** is growing for green reasons.
Tom's **design clients** would stop asking for free machine-made logos.
do: Finish the **crane supervisor** course already booked for spring.
Keep using the **AI assistant** for method statements and material lists.
Save **400 a month** toward a deposit.
S0.quote: I'm the rare builder who'd be a bit disappointed if AI fizzled, and still have more work than I can handle.
fieldNote: He has a **full order book** and five months saved, so calm fits.
He is an early **AI user**, yet happy for the hype to fail.
Tom's **freelance work** is the household's soft spot.

steps.text: Keep the timber crew going on the primary school job
Finish the crane supervisor course booked for spring
Save 400 a month toward a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for training money and for unions to get in early, not after the layoffs. I'd also say, as someone who already uses the tools, that they make a decent builder faster, not useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly good. The thinking AI takes the paperwork I hate, and robots are slow to reach site work. For Tom, it's harder: freelance logo work would dry up, though his teaching would mostly hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push my firm to let me trial the new planning tools first, so I become the person who sets them up for other crews. Join the union and get on its technology committee. Help Tom shift more of his hours into teaching design, which I think lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Tom, a bit excited for me. It's a strange mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your household income is Tom's freelance work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third, maybe less. If his freelance went, we'd tighten up, but we'd pay the rent. If Tom (his boyfriend) loses his logo clients, we eat cheaper, but we still pay the rent on my timber wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited for yourself and worried for Tom. How do you talk about that at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. I try not to be cheerful about AI at dinner. He's said once or twice that it's easy for me, and he's not wrong.

say: I'd call for **training money** and early union involvement.
I'd tell people the tools make a decent builder **faster, not useless**.
think: The thinking AI takes the **paperwork** I hate, and robots come slowly.
Tom's **freelance logos** would dry up, but his teaching mostly holds.
do: Trial the firm's new **planning tools** first and set them up for other crews.
Help Tom move more hours into **teaching design**.
feel: **Uneasy** for Tom and quietly **excited** for himself.
S1.quote: If Tom (his boyfriend) loses his logo clients, we eat cheaper, but we still pay the rent on my timber wages.
fieldNote: His own job **gains** from this picture; the household risk is a **third of income**.
He is careful about **sounding cheerful** at home.
He pairs early adoption with **union** involvement, not against it.

steps.text: Volunteer to trial the firm's AI planning tools first
Help Tom move more hours into teaching design

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments are about to find out whether they meant anything they said about a fair transition. I'd be campaigning for a basic income, because two years isn't enough for half the country to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mass-timber panels are made in a factory and fitted on a grid, so they're about the easiest building work a robot could learn. I'd give my crew until about 2031. My bet is I could be the one running the robot crew, but there'd be one of me where there are six of us now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start now on anything that gets me closer to running machines: the crane ticket, then a robotics operator course as soon as one exists. Save 600 a month, because Tom's freelance would be gone within the year. And I'd put my name forward to the union to negotiate how robot crews get staffed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for myself so much, more for the five people on my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas, mostly, he's forty-five and he's been on timber since before I could drive. I could end up supervising the robot that replaces Jonas (his oldest crew mate), and I don't know how I'd look at him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 2028 to 2031 look like for you, those three years before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy and strange. The planning would all be AI, so the office would shrink, but we'd still be on the tools. I'd use those years to get every ticket I can and to save, because once the robots land, the jobs left will go to people who can run them.

say: I'd test whether governments meant their promises of a **fair transition**.
I'd campaign for a **basic income** because two years is too short.
think: Factory-made panels are **easy work for robots**, likely by about 2031.
I might run the **robot crew**, but one of me replaces six of us.
do: Get the crane ticket, then a **robotics operator** course once one exists.
Save **600 a month** as Tom's freelance work disappears.
Help the union **negotiate** how robot crews are staffed.
feel: **Anxious**, more for his five crew mates than for himself.
S2.quote: I could end up supervising the robot that replaces Jonas (his oldest crew mate), and I don't know how I'd look at him.
fieldNote: He expects his **crew** to shrink sharply but sees a path for himself.
Tom's freelance income going is a real **household** hit, softened by teaching.
The thought of **supervising** Jonas's replacement clearly troubles him.

steps.text: Take a robotics operator course as soon as one opens
Save 600 a month while Tom's freelance work fades

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this decently if we start now: training funds, union deals on robot crews, help for older workers. I'd be pretty vocal about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2031 and robots around 2034 gives me seven or eight years on the tools, and I'd be thirty-five. That's time to move up to running machines and to help Tom land somewhere solid. I think we'd come through fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the crane ticket, then a site management course over two years. Ask the firm to make me their lead on robot trials when they come. Start putting 300 a month into a pension, which I've never done properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a pension now, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if my working years get shorter, the ones I've got need to count. Five years of warning made me open the pension letter I've been ignoring since I was twenty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Jonas in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time. Five years means he could move to the factory side, making the panels, or into fire-safety checks. I'd push the firm to pay for that.

say: I'd say five years is enough if we start **training funds** now.
I'd push for **union deals** on robot crews and help for older workers.
think: I'd have about **eight years** on the tools before robots arrive.
That's time to move into **running machines** and help Tom settle.
do: Finish the crane ticket and a two-year **site management** course.
Ask to lead the firm's **robot trials**.
Pay **300 a month** into a pension.
S3.quote: Five years of warning made me open the pension letter I've been ignoring since I was twenty-two.
fieldNote: With **eight years** of runway his own work feels safe for now.
The pension decision shows a **long-term** turn in his thinking.
He keeps pushing for **older crew mates** like Jonas.

steps.text: Complete a two-year site management course
Ask to lead the firm's robot trials on site
Pay 300 a month into a pension

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty if we're serious, and I'd use it to argue for a proper national retraining plan for building trades. I'd also tell young people to keep coming into construction, because the next fifteen years still need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one's good for me. I'd be forty by the time robots could do timber work, and by then I'd want to be running a site anyway. Tom has ten years to move fully into teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep building and keep learning. Do site management in years two to four, then maybe a part-time engineering degree. And buy a flat with Tom in the next couple of years, because we'd finally have a clear runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even quietly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a school leaver who asked if they should do carpentry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do it, but learn the computers too. I'd tell a sixteen-year-old to learn timber with their hands and robots with their head, because they'll need both by forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd get complacent with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably for others, not for me. I'm the one who books courses before the email's even finished. Tom says I treat the future like a timetable.

say: I'd push for a **national retraining plan** for building trades.
I'd tell young people construction still needs them for **fifteen years**.
think: Robots reach timber work at about **forty**, when I'd be running sites anyway.
Tom has **ten years** to move fully into teaching.
do: Study **site management** in years two to four.
Buy a **flat** with Tom within two years.
S4.quote: I'd tell a sixteen-year-old to learn timber with their hands and robots with their head, because they'll need both by forty.
fieldNote: Secure, adaptive and young, he sees a decade as a **ladder**, not a threat.
Buying a flat signals real **confidence** in his income.
His advice to young people is **hands and head**, both.

steps.text: Keep leading timber crews on school and library jobs
Study site management, then part-time engineering
Buy a flat with Tom within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for me so much as for the crew and for Tom. What would help is paid robotics training that builders can actually get into, and a union agreement on how many people stay on a robot crew. I'm not scared of robots putting up timber, I'm scared of a site where I'm the only person left to say good morning to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people like me should feel guilty. I'm getting ahead by learning the tools that might push my mates out. I don't think it's wrong, but it isn't simple either.
